items.summary: Voted for two budget-committee bills: SB 125 (2023), letting regions use state transit capital funds for operating costs under an accountability program after the Governor's May proposal offered no transit aid (Senate 32–7; signed 2023-07-10), and AB 117, requiring a state loan of up to $590 million for operating loans to four Bay Area transit operators (Senate 28–9; signed 2026-02-19); no measured outcome recorded as of 2026-11-03.
items.title: State transit funding: 2023 transportation budget trailer bill (SB 125) and Bay Area transit loan law (AB 117)

citations.quote: Transportation budget trailer bill.
`Committee on Budget and Fiscal Review`	`LEAD_AUTHOR`

The bill would authorize a regional transportation planning agency, subject to compliance with the requirements described below, to use those moneys to fund transit operating expenses within its jurisdiction and for the transformative capital improvements authorized under the Transit and Intercity Rail Capital Program, as specified.
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20230SB12596CHP (SB 125, Chaptered, 2023-07-10), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_7371.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest (2)

citations.quote: The bill would require the Transportation Agency to develop and administer an accountability program to govern the distribution of funds
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20230SB12596CHP (SB 125, Chaptered, 2023-07-10), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_7371.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest (2)

citations.quote: While Newsom’s May budget proposal failed to provide any assistance for transit agencies facing a “fiscal cliff,” and delayed $2 billion in construction projects, the Legislature rejected that move and proposed an additional $1.1 billion over the next three years from the state’s cap-and-trade funds.
Assembly amendments concurred in. (Ayes 32. Noes  7. Page 1772.) Ordered to engrossing and enrolling.
Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter 54, Statutes of 2023.
`Committee on Budget`	`LEAD_AUTHOR`

This bill would require, on or before July 1, 2026, the Transportation Agency, subject to various requirements, to loan to the Metropolitan Transportation Commission up to $590,000,000 of funding approved under the program for projects within the San Francisco Bay area.
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20250AB11796CHP (AB 117, Chaptered, 2026-02-19), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_11217.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest

citations.quote: conditions, for public transit operating purposes to the San Francisco Bay Area Rapid Transit District, the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, the Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board, and the Alameda-Contra Costa Transit District.
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20250AB11796CHP (AB 117, Chaptered, 2026-02-19), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_11217.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest

citations.quote: Read third time. Passed. Ordered to the Assembly. (Ayes 28. Noes  9. Page 3425.).

citations.locator: BILL_DETAIL_VOTE_TBL, bill_id 202520260AB117, Senate floor 2026-02-19, vote 1003 (third reading)

citations.quote: Chaptered by Secretary of State - Chapter 6, Statutes of 2026.
Transit agencies will receive a total of $5.1 billion over four years, though the money will be subject to accountability measures and state oversight.

Sen. Scott Wiener, a Democrat from San Francisco who has been leading the charge to fend off the transit “fiscal cliff,” said the deal would cover a significant portion of transit systems’ collective operating deficit, but said the state should use more federal highway money to fund transit operations.

According to state legislation passed in June, the $750 million loan is cemented into the budget, but the duration and terms of the loan are to be determined in separate “budget trailing” legislation.

Eventually, just before adjournment, Newsom said he would “offer short-term financial assistance to support Bay Area transit agencies with hundreds of millions of dollars,” but he didn’t give an exact number.
In 2025, for instance, Wiener secured an emergency state loan for Muni, BART and Caltrain, intended to stabilize them until the regional transit measures passes.

items.summary: Authored SB 35 with principal co-author Sen. Atkins, creating a streamlined, ministerial approval process for qualifying multifamily housing in localities short of their housing-permit targets until January 1, 2026; signed 2017-09-29 (Assembly 47–27, Senate concurrence 23–14), and a 2023 Senate floor analysis counted 19,239 SB 35 units in 2018–2021 local progress reports, 60% affordable to lower-income households.
items.title: SB 35: streamlined approval for qualifying multifamily housing (2017)

citations.quote: `Atkins`	`PRINCIPAL_COAUTHOR`

This bill would authorize a development proponent to submit an application for a multifamily housing development, which satisfies specified planning objective standards, that is subject to a streamlined, ministerial approval process, as provided, and not subject to a conditional use permit.
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20170SB3587CHP (Chaptered, 2017-09-29), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_9824.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest (2)

citations.quote: The bill would repeal these provisions as of January 1, 2026.
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20170SB3587CHP (Chaptered, 2017-09-29), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_9824.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest (2)

citations.quote: In 2017, SB 35 (Wiener) created a streamlined approval process for infill projects with two or more residential units in localities that have failed to issue sufficient housing permits to meet their RHNA.
citations.locator: BILL_ANALYSIS_TBL row 368052 (SB 423, Sen. Floor Analyses, Unfinished Business, 2023-09-08), text file BILL_ANALYSIS_TBL_11658.lob, Background

citations.quote: Read third time. Passed. (Ayes 47. Noes 27. Page 3420.) Ordered to the Senate.
Assembly amendments concurred in. (Ayes 23. Noes 14. Page 2958.) Ordered to engrossing and enrolling.
Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter 366, Statutes of 2017.

According to data provided by local governments in their annual progress reports (APRs) between 2018 and 2021 statewide, SB 35 has resulted in 19,239 units, 60% of which are affordable to lower-income households.

items.summary: Authored SB 1047, the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act, with co-authors Sens. Roth, Rubio and Stern, requiring developers of covered AI models to implement full-shutdown capability, written safety and security protocols and annual third-party audits; vetoed by the Governor 2024-09-29 after Assembly 48–16 and Senate concurrence 30–9 votes; no measured outcome recorded as of 2026-11-03.
items.title: SB 1047: safety requirements for frontier AI model developers (2024)

citations.quote: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act.
`Roth`	`COAUTHOR`
`Rubio`	`COAUTHOR`
`Stern`	`COAUTHOR`

require that a developer, before beginning to initially train a covered model, as defined, comply with various requirements, including implementing the capability to promptly enact a full shutdown, as defined, and implement a written and separate safety and security protocol, as specified.
citations.locator: BILL_VERSION_TBL row 20230SB104788ENR (Enrolled, 2024-09-03), text file BILL_VERSION_TBL_19202.lob, Legislative Counsel's Digest

citations.quote: The bill would require a developer, beginning January 1, 2026, to annually retain a third-party auditor to perform an independent audit of compliance with those provisions, as prescribed.

items.summary: Authored SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, with co-author Sen.
